Copper Quarterly January 2012 # Executive Summary ## Fundamentals support while investors lie in wait - The CRU view remains fundamentally unchanged from that which we presented in October. Large deficits in 2012 and into H1 2013 will drive already depleted stocks down to critically low levels and lead to prices rising back towards $10,000/t by Q2 2013. - The one change over the situation three months ago is that the Eurozone debt crisis has been left to fester, rather than the nettle being grasped by Eurozone politicians. As a result, some of the heat has been taken out of investor interest in copper and other “risky assets”. As more clarity on the macroeconomic outlook emerges as the year progresses, we expect to see some of this money come back into the market to boost the copper price. - Supply growth in 2012 will be driven by new projects and the ramping up of projects that came on in 2011. However, this means that mine production this year will only barely exceed the levels achieved in 2010. - We estimate that the refined market in 2011 was in deficit by almost 400,000t and, given the sluggish growth in mine output, in 2012 faces a similar sized deficit. With more of the deficit in 2011 having been fed by off-warrant inventory, reported stock levels are now expected to remain above the critical 1.2 weeks ratio to consumption. As a result of this and a slow return of investor money, prices will only rise back above $9,000/t on average by Q3 2012 and average around $8,830/t ($4.00/lb) for the year. - In 2013, supply growth will really start to make its presence felt, with refined output forecast to rise by 6.5%. However, this will allow consumption growth to double, keeping the market in deficit in H1. As stocks are driven down to critically low levels, prices should rise towards $10,000/t in Q2. New mine projects will push the market into surplus in H2 and prices will come off somewhat, leaving the 2013 annual average price forecast at $9,390/t ($4.25/lb). - The refined market will move into progressively larger surpluses over the 2014-2016 period, reaching 570,000t in 2016. Stock levels will therefore increase to 3.7 weeks of consumption by 2016 on a reported stocks basis. This will replenish stocks throughout the supply chain, with the price falling back to average around $7,400/t ($3.36/lb) by the end of the outlook period. |Table I: LME Copper|price

However, by 2015-16 consumption is below previous estimates, as we forecast increased substitution to aluminium wire and cable. As a result of lower Chinese imports of semis, refined consumption in the rest of Asia, particularly Korea and Taiwan, has been reduced in 2012-13. European consumption in 2012 is also down compared to October by 125,000t and by over 200,000t in 2013-16 due to a worse economic outlook. **Supply** : Mine disruptions and project delays have resulted in a lowering of our refined production estimate for 2013 by 160,000t compared to previous forecasts. The reduction widens to over 300,000t in 2014-15, as we have raised the disruption allowance to account for the log-jam effect from the unprecedented growth in mine output. Higher output from the bunching of delayed mine projects results in the gap falling to 125,000t by 2016. **Prices** : Prices for 2012 have been lowered by $500/t and by $685/t in 2013 as a result of a slower decline in stock to critically low levels. This reduction increases to about $1,800/t in 2015-16, as emerging surpluses lead to higher stock levels by 2016. ### Macroeconomic concerns dominate short term outlook Having shed some of the investor money in the market in September 2011, the copper market was stuck in a trading band between $6,800/t and just over $8,000/t in Q4. Oscillations were largely driven by developments in the on-going Eurozone debt debacle, which also capped rallies. Price movements had little or no relationship to developments in the market fundamentals. The start and finish of the Grasberg and Cerro Verde strikes was associated with minimal price movements, despite Grasberg alone accounting for an estimated 80,000t of lost mine output in Q4 2011 compared to our forecast in July. Also, the release of November import figures on 21st December showed that China imported a record amount of copper in all forms (see the chart below), but the news was associated with only a modest $300/t rally in the LME price. The 10th January release of preliminary Chinese import figures for December showed a 12% m-o-m rise in wrought and unwrought copper, but was related to an even smaller increase in the price. onfidential Copper Quarterly January 2012 Executive Summary 3 At the low end of the trading range, however, the copper market does remain well supported by strong fundamentals from a combination of low stocks, growing (though slowing) consumption and struggling mine production. The latter two combined to create an estimated global refined market deficit of 390,000t for 2011 as a whole, with the bulk of the drawdown happening in H2. The low levels of stocks throughout the supply chain was highlighted by the decline of more than 100,000t in reported stocks in Q4, much of which we believe went to China to help feed the rise in imports seen in the final quarter of 2011. ### Chinese imports up ahead of the New Year... Given the rise in the December preliminary figures noted above, we now estimate that when Chinese cathode imports in Q4 are confirmed they will total over 1Mt. This would be the second highest quarterly total ever and more than 300,000t higher than in Q3. We believe that this increase was for a combination of immediate consumption and stocking. These came from, on the one hand, a decline in Chinese domestic refined output of 125,000t q-o-q in Q4. On the other hand, some scrap units were held back by scrap traders following the sharp fall in the copper price in September, forcing semi-fabricators to use more cathode. The remaining increase in imported metal we account for by the usual seasonal stocking ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year, mostly by traders. Traders normally use bonded warehouses to park metal before shipping it to customers, because they do not need to pay 17% VAT until they withdraw the metal from the bonded warehouse. Therefore, an RMB10,000/t increase in the copper price would cost a trader a further RMB1,700/t in VAT. Despite the rise in imports, bonded stocks rose by only 50,000t from the end of September to around 300,000t by mid-January. At the same time, the average copper price in China fell by 16% (over RMB10,000/t) q-o-q in the final quarter of 2011. We suspect that some traders are betting on the price rising in Q1 2012 and therefore moved metal straight into non-bonded warehouses at the lower prices in Q4. In addition to traders restocking, we be

lieve there may have been an increase in stocks held at semi-fabricators.  Many semis plants in China take a full week off for the New Year holiday, which begins on 23<sup>rd</sup> January.  Furthermore, the period following the New Year is associated with the start of the highest seasonal demand period in the year.  Semi-fabricators have traditionally stocked up on cathode to hit the ground running to meet the higher demand following the holiday. Last year, with prices heading towards a record on the LME, consumers actually destocked.  This year though, the lower prices in Q4 may have allowed some fabricators to employ the same amount of working capital to increase stock levels above the levels they held in Q3. 

We do not consider that the collateral stock phenomenon played much of a role in the increase in imports.  Collateral stocks helped drive import growth last year when speculators used copper imports as collateral for financing of other activities.  Regulatory changes seem to have reined in this practice. 

### ...and Chinese consumption growth to dwarf all others in 2012 

We forecast that Chinese consumption growth of refined copper will accelerate in 2012 to 7.5% from the 5.9% growth we estimate for 2011.  We expect that seasonally stronger demand will come through in Q2 2012.  In addition, the decline in inflation and GDP growth throughout 2011 will allow the government to further loosen monetary policy to support domestic demand

A destocking phase at copper consuming end-users of semi-fabricated products, such as domestic appliance manufacturers, is expected to finish in Q1, which should also boost refined consumption as demand for semis picks up again. Our estimates and forecasts of 2011 and 2012 consumption are stronger than we were forecasting in October, with 2012 also expected to be aided by a boost from completions of the 10M “affordable housing” units started last year. Consumption is anticipated to be over 260,000t higher in 2012 than we had forecast three months ago and this growth will overshadow changes in the rest of the world (see chart below). This strong performance by China’s domestic fabricating industry will lead to a lower import requirements for semi-fabricated products. This will hit semis production, and therefore refined copper consumption, in Korea and Taiwan in particular, the largest suppliers of semis to China. We now expect to see refined consumption falling in Korea by a further 8% on top of the 5% decline we estimate for 2011. Taiwan faces a similar story with consumption down by 7.2% in 2012, adding to the 6% fall we calculate for 2011. The only other major market that we predict will grow substantially due to underlying demand in 2012 will be Russia. Robust production of wire and cable for domestic consumption means we now forecast that Russian refined consumption in 2012 will grow by 5%. Following the 42% growth in 2011, due to the reimpostion of the export tax on cathode and the consequent increase in wirerod production for export, consumption in Russia will be back up to just below the 2008 peak. Japan is expected to register growth of 2%, but this is more on account of the comparison being made with a year in which consumption declined in the wake of the March earthquake and tsunami. In other major consuming markets we have reduced forecasts across the board this year. Crisis-hit Europe has taken the biggest knock to the tune of a collective 125,000t from consumption in 2012 compared to our October forecast. The crisis is at heart one of balance of payments imbalances but the political energy has thus far been devoted towards dealing with the symptom of government debt. Consumption growth did hold up relatively well in Europe in Q4 2011. However, the confusion of the politicians is reducing the visibility of copper market consumers, leading to a reining in of orders by copper containing end-use customers that is now cascading back to semi-fabricators. Proportionally the biggest hit has been taken by the southern European countries at the epicentre of the crisis, particularly Italy and Spain. However, northern Europe has not been spared, as lower demand for copper containing goods leads to lower semis exports and therefore refined consumption in countries in the north. Germany is therefore forecast to suffer the largest absolute decline. We also forecast a slight decline in US refined consumption, as anaemic economic growth coupled with Russian wirerod imports curbs domestic semis production. ### Sluggish supply growth to leave market in deficit in 2012... Refined copper production edged higher by just 0.1% in 2011 to 18.8Mt, as mine production fell by an estimated 2.45% to 15.62Mt, its lowest level for 3 years. Refined output was maintained only due to increased use of scrap as a raw material. Mine production was just 0.8% higher than in 2008, as severe disruptions to output more than offset gains from project start-ups. The strikes at the Grasberg and Cerro Verde mines lasted well into December, and output has yet to return to normal levels at Grasberg. The problem of inadequate infrastructure, particularly water and power is also becoming more significant. New production from mining projects is set to increase this year, with 20 greenfield operations to be commissioned, including Salobo and Antapaccay. Further increases in mine production will come from the ramp ups taking place at the major brownfield projects which began last year, namely Los Bronces and Antamina. In addition, strike hit operations (which included the world number 1 and 2 mines) should be able to operate fully this year, leading to our forecast of mine production growth of 3.0% to 16.1Mt and an increase in refined output of 2.3% to 19.2Mt. This 2012 production growth c

ompares to a forecast of consumption of 2.2%, which leaves the market in a deficit of over 380,000t. Stocks should decline as a result, but remain above critically low levels of under 1.2 weeks for reported stocks. Financial turmoil is expected to remain a feature this year, so that fickle investor behaviour will continue to drive volatility like it did in Q4 2011. However, as the year progresses and some clarity on the global macroeconomic outlook emerges, we expect to see investors increase their exposure to risk assets such as copper. Therefore, as fundamental, macroeconomic and financial factors will all be moving in the same direction, we forecast that the price will rise throughout 2012 to average $8,826/t, up from a quarterly average of $8,300/t in Q1 to $9,240/t by Q4. ### ...before supply growth shifts market into surpluses from H2 2013 and beyond However, 2013 is set to be the year in which the new wave of copper projects really begins to make its presence felt. We forecast that projects will drive a 6.6% increase in mine production to 17.2Mt next year, leading to refined output growth of 6.5%. In 2013 we expect to see 26 greenfield and 20 brownfield projects start up, most notably the Oyu Tolgoi project in Mongolia and the Mina Ministro Hales and Caserones-Regalito concentrates projects in Chile. We then expect to see several more years of strong growth in mined copper production with annual increases of 4.5-5.8%, as projects continue to come on stream and ramp up to full production. This will fuel refined growth of 4.6-6.1% per year over the remainder of the outlook period. #### Prices to peak in 2013, as deficits lower stocks and tighten the market LME cash price and supply/demand balance*, quarterly, 2005-2013 Forecast

### Key risks to the price outlook In 2012 risks to the price around the base case are biased 2:1 to the upside, as the range forecast in the chart at the top of the next page demonstrates. Downside macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are more than offset by the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. By 2013, the risks become slightly less biased, but remain to the upside throughout the remainder of the forecast period driven principally by production risks. ##### **Production risks** All production risks to the price are to the upside. The first is that insufficient availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge. Should financial market stress lead to a double dip recession in the Eurozone and the USA, financing for copper mine projects due on stream over the next five years would likely be affected, leading to further delays.  Even the majors, who are currently flush with cash, may ramp up their projects more slowly or otherwise defer some of the production due on stream from their projects. 

##### **Macroeconomic and financial risks** 

The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the current financial market turmoil will play out, both in terms of the direct impact of financial players on the copper price and the indirect effects of a financial crisis in Europe on the wider economy and on refined consumption. Markets seem to be coming to accept that the Eurozone crisis has a long way to run.  That said, there are lingering concerns regarding a European recession and the extent to which it might affect the health of banks and economic activity in the rest of the world.  On the other hand, it now seems more likely that economic growth in both the US and China will continue at current rates, rather than decelerating.  This is positive for growth in those emerging markets which export to these two large economies. 

##### **Consumption risks** 

##### **Downside** 

Aluminium substitution has long been a threat to copper demand, with aluminium rods being a viable and cheaper choice with which to replace copper rods for wire and cable manufacture. However, in 2012, the wire and cable manufacturers may start to find aluminium wirerod harder to get hold of, and may be forced to use greater quantities of copper wirerod as a raw material. Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply, leading to depressed prices which are currently hovering at around $2,200/t on the LME.  According to CRU’s aluminium production cost curve, around 30% of the aluminium smelting industry has costs that exceed current prices, and indeed, plant closures have

Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth.  In this Quarterly, we now expect that aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015.  CRU also forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-ma

king. 

The potential impact of political turmoil resulting in financial market stress and another serious recession in the Eurozone and/or the USA is also a major risk.  Although the emerging markets are performing well, driven by domestic demand, there are concerns about inflationary pressures. Copper consumption would be negatively affected by emerging market governments introducing anti-inflationary policies which would dent economic growth. 

##### **Upside** 

The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) would lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 

Any double-dip would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries, by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 

Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes at prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of currency appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification.
